answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**Temporal Proximity Alone Does Not Establish Causation Unless the Timing Is Unusually Suggestive.**

A prima facie case of retaliation requires proof that (1) the plaintiff engaged in protected activity, (2) the employer took adverse action, and (3) a causal link connects the two. *Kachmar v. SunGard Data Sys., Inc.*, 109 F.3d 173, 177 (3d Cir. 1997); *Daniels v. Sch. Dist. of Phila.*, 776 F.3d 181, 193 (3d Cir. 2015). Sequence is not causation. Under Title VII, the plaintiff ultimately must prove that retaliation was a but-for cause of the challenged action. *Univ. of Tex. Sw. Med. Ctr. v. Nassar*, 570 U.S. 338, 362 (2013). Although the prima facie burden is lighter, the plaintiff still must produce evidence sufficient to raise an inference that the protected activity was the likely reason for the adverse action. *Carvalho-Grevious v. Del. State Univ.*, 851 F.3d 249, 259 (3d Cir. 2017).

When a plaintiff relies on timing alone, the timing must be "unusually suggestive" of retaliatory motive before a causal link will be inferred. *Krouse v. Am. Sterilizer Co.*, 126 F.3d 494, 503 (3d Cir. 1997). *Krouse* held that an interval of roughly nineteen months did not permit that inference. *Id.* at 503–04. The Supreme Court has likewise recognized that cases accepting temporal proximity as sufficient evidence of causality require that the proximity be "very close," and that action taken 20 months later "suggests, by itself, no causality at all." *Clark Cnty. Sch. Dist. v. Breeden*, 532 U.S. 268, 273–74 (2001) (per curiam).

This Court has applied the same principle to far shorter intervals. In *Williams v. Philadelphia Housing Authority Police Department*, 380 F.3d 751, 760 (3d Cir. 2004), a gap of about two months was not unusually suggestive. And in *LeBoon v. Lancaster Jewish Community Center Ass'n*, 503 F.3d 217, 233 (3d Cir. 2007), the Court explained that, although no bright-line rule governs, "a gap of three months between the protected activity and the adverse action, without more, cannot create an inference of causation and defeat summary judgment." *See also Jones v. Se. Pa. Transp. Auth.*, 796 F.3d 323, 330 (3d Cir. 2015) (interval of several months was not unusually suggestive).

Absent unusually suggestive timing, the plaintiff must supply something more, such as intervening antagonism, retaliatory animus, inconsistencies in the employer's explanation, or other record evidence supporting an inference of causation. *See Marra v. Phila. Hous. Auth.*, 497 F.3d 286, 302 (3d Cir. 2007); *Farrell v. Planters Lifesavers Co.*, 206 F.3d 271, 279–81 (3d Cir. 2000). The inquiry is contextual. The mere passage of time is not conclusive proof against retaliation, *Kachmar*, 109 F.3d at 178, and timing may be weighed together with other evidence, *Farrell*, 206 F.3d at 280–81. But that flexibility permits a plaintiff to prove causation through additional evidence; it does not excuse the failure to produce any when the timing is not itself unusually suggestive.

Here, Plaintiff relies on the bare interval of [length of interval] between [protected activity] and [adverse action]. [Record citation.] That interval is not unusually suggestive. Nor has Plaintiff identified a pattern of intervening antagonism, a statement reflecting retaliatory animus, a material inconsistency in Defendant's stated reason, or any other evidence linking the two events. [Record citations.] A jury could connect them only by assuming that because one followed the other, the first caused the second. This Court's precedent does not permit that inference on timing of this kind. Because Plaintiff cannot establish causation, [he/she] cannot make out a prima facie case, and this Court should [affirm the entry of summary judgment for Defendant].
